title: Who Gets the Flu Shot?
hook: Predicting H1N1 and seasonal flu vaccine uptake from a national survey of 26,707 people

slides.title: Who Gets the Flu Shot?
slides.subtitle: DrivenData "Flu Shot Learning" competition
slides.narration: This one's a machine learning competition. Divyesh used a US national survey to predict who got the H1N1 flu vaccine and who got the seasonal one.

slides.title: The problem
bullets: Data from the 2009 U.S. National H1N1 Flu Survey
Two separate yes/no targets: the H1N1 vaccine and the seasonal flu vaccine
35 features covering opinions, health behaviours, demographics and employment
Scored by ROC AUC, so each person needs a probability, not just a yes or no
slides.narration: For each respondent, the model has to estimate how likely they were to get each vaccine, based on their opinions, habits and background.

slides.title: The data at a glance
bullets: H1N1 is imbalanced and seasonal is close to balanced, so each target is handled differently
Heavy missing data: employment occupation 50.4%, industry 49.9%, health insurance 46.0%
slides.narration: Only about one in five people got the H1N1 shot, while nearly half got the seasonal one. Some columns were missing for half of all respondents.

slides.title: Missing data isn't random
bullets: Occupation is missing for 100% of unemployed people and those not in the labour force
It's missing for only 2.4% of employed people
85.4% of respondents aged 65+ had no occupation, consistent with retirement
So the gaps were filled as "Retired" (age 65+) or "Unknown". The fact that a value is missing becomes a signal instead of being lost
slides.narration: A blank occupation usually means the person isn't working. Instead of guessing, Divyesh filled the gaps in a way that keeps that meaning.

slides.title: What the statistics showed
bullets: Chi-square and Cramér's V tests run on all 12 categorical features against both targets
Age matters a lot for the seasonal shot but barely at all for H1N1
Occupation and industry are the categorical features most strongly linked to both targets
slides.narration: Age turned out to be a big driver of seasonal vaccination but almost irrelevant for H1N1. That's a good reason to model the two targets separately.

slides.title: The pipeline

steps.label: Clean
steps.detail: Domain-aware filling for employment fields, IterativeImputer for numeric gaps

steps.label: Engineer
steps.detail: 9 new features, e.g. combined doctor-recommendation score, household size, age × income

steps.label: Model
steps.detail: Random Forest, XGBoost and CatBoost, one model per target, on a stratified 80/20 split (21,365 / 5,342)

steps.label: Tune
steps.detail: Optuna: 50 trials per target, scored by 5-fold stratified cross-validated AUC

slides.narration: The steps were: clean the data carefully, add new features, compare three model families, and then tune the best one with Optuna.

slides.title: Model comparison on the hold-out set
slides.unit: Mean ROC AUC across both targets (higher is better)
slides.narration: All three model families ended up within a hundredth of each other in AUC, and tuning added very little. That says the next gains will come from better features, not a different model.

slides.title: What drives H1N1 vaccination
bullets: A doctor's recommendation is the single strongest predictor
Opinions about risk and vaccine effectiveness come next, ahead of demographics
slides.narration: The biggest factor was simple: did a doctor recommend the vaccine? After that came how risky people thought the flu was and whether they believed the vaccine works.

slides.title: Limitations and lessons
bullets: Scores are from an internal hold-out split, not the competition leaderboard
Label encoding treats categories as ordered numbers; one-hot or target encoding may do better
Optuna changed AUC by only about ±0.001, so model choice wasn't the bottleneck
Biggest lesson: understand why data is missing before you fill it
slides.narration: He's honest about the limits. These are internal scores, the encoding could be better, and tuning hardly moved the needle. The real win came from understanding the missing data.
